extracted.intended_audience: educated American political figures, friends, and correspondents (late 18th century); readers of Jefferson's private/public letters
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and extraction of prescriptive guidance, legal rules, and practical advice from Thomas Jefferson's letters (personal, legal, diplomatic, and political). Useful for historians, legal scholars, and editorial projects compiling historical correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion — divest prejudice and submit claims to reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Divest yourself of all bias in favor of novelty and singularity of opinion; shake off fears and servile prejudices; fix reason firmly in her seat and call to her tribunal every fact and opinion. Question with boldness even the existence of a God; your own reason is the only oracle given you by Heaven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept or reject religious claims because others do. Examine pretensions to inspiration and judge them by evidence and probability rather than authority or ecclesiastical decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read religious histories like secular histories
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the Bible 'as you would read Livy or Tacitus' — accept facts within the ordinary course of nature on authorial authority as you would in secular histories; treat extraordinary claims differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary natural facts may be believed on the writer's authority; facts contradicting laws of nature require more careful examination and stronger evidence (see example of Joshua's sun standing still).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary (miraculous) claims require stronger evidentiary support
rubrics_metrics.description: Those facts in the Bible which contradict the laws of nature must be examined with more care and under a variety of faces. Examine the writer's pretension to inspiration and whether that evidence is stronger than the improbability of a change in natural law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare probabilities: is arrest of earth's motion or the evidence for it more consistent with natural laws? Use your astronomical/empirical knowledge in weighing such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider opposing pretensions concerning Jesus candidly
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep in view opposing pretensions: (1) that Jesus was divine, born of a virgin, performed miracles and ascended bodily; (2) that he was a man of illegitimate birth, enthusiastic mind, punished for sedition. Examine these claims with the same critical standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult relevant legal/historical sources (e.g., Roman law references cited) and modern critical works (books he referenced under 'Religion') but keep reason on the watch in all readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include apocryphal/‘pseudo-evangelists’ in assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Read all histories of Christ, including those ecclesiastics have decided to be Pseudo-evangelists, because they 'pretended to inspiration as much as the others' and their pretensions must be judged by your own reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not defer to ecclesiastical judgments about authenticity; seek extant collections (Fabricius referenced) and weigh their claims alongside canonical texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel — generally advisable later in life; harms of youthful travel
rubrics_metrics.description: Travelling makes men wiser but less happy; sober-age travel gathers useful knowledge, but young men who travel are exposed to stronger inconveniences, weakened affections, idleness, and habits incompatible with industry and virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer learning at home through repeated, just observations; if you travel, take much exercise (on foot) and cultivate health and industry to avoid the dregs of fleeting pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wills rule — 'the first deed and last will must always prevail'
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of multiple testamentary instruments, the general rule is that the first deed and the last will prevail; later wills override earlier inconsistent dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where conflict arises, examine whether later will is validly executed and whether earlier deeds or wills contain controlling language; absent special circumstances, the last will should control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devise phrasing — words of inheritance and the meaning of 'estate'
rubrics_metrics.description: A devise to a person without the words 'and to his heirs' may still create a fee simple when the term 'estate' is used; 'estate' has been repeatedly decided to be descriptive of the quantum of interest devised as well as of its locality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If words of inheritance are absent, determine whether 'estate' or other language supplies the necessary intent for fee simple; copy and examine the exact words of the will to decide interest (might result in life estate for some tracts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal government design principles
rubrics_metrics.description: States should preserve their sovereignty in matters concerning themselves alone; whatever concerns another State or foreign nation should vest in federal sovereignty. The exercise of federal sovereignty should be divided into three bodies: legislative, executive, and judiciary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additionally, provide some peaceable means for the federal head to enforce compliance by the States; this balance between union (foreign affairs) and state separateness (domestic matters) is central to constitutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diplomatic/prisoner-redemption policy — secrecy and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: In redeeming captives at Algiers, do not let the idea of public interest in their redemption transpire; do not accept the unusually high 'Spanish price,' and set aside a distinct fund (estimate provided: $500 per prisoner) before proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Destroy any public notion of intending to redeem prisoners to avoid making one's vessels targets; proceed only when treasury commissioners place necessary funds under the minister's orders; be cautious about pledging to families that redemption is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical educational aids — prefer simple, hands-on tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Wood is as good as ivory for geometric demonstration diagrams; making figures themselves (from veneer or pasteboard) can improve students' understanding; only simple tools (penknife, wooden rule) may be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider having students construct diagrams themselves to reconcile physical breadth of models with the abstraction of mathematical lines; if preferred, the correspondent can commission them abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion and reform — power of open discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion (mobs, assemblies, parliamentary protest) has effected significant reform in France by constraining royal authority and promoting provincial assemblies chosen by the people; the 'license of speaking' against government has been widely exercised without punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censuring or limiting public debate (e.g., 'tying up the tongues' of assembly members) is criticized; open discussion is preferable and can be a powerful check on authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic policy preference — favor agriculture over speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Peace and agriculture are preferable to war and speculative commerce; speculation yields fugacious wealth and gambling spirit, whereas husbandry produces permanent improvement, quiet life, and orderly conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit commerce to removing superfluous produce; avoid overtrading and becoming maritime speculators, which would divert the republic from its wisest pursuit (agriculture).
